Menopause and the midlife body change training reality for half the population, and sport science has barely studied it ⚠️. If practice is lifelong, the program can't design only for the 25-year-old male body the research over-sampled. How does the program push honest, life-stage-specific practice knowledge across the whole arc — and is the under-studied midlife female athlete a research gap Toronto could actually help close?

For a huge share of people, "sport" is a wound — the kid picked last, the fat kid in gym class, the one the scale-and-shame culture drove out for good (SP51). A body-mastery program that shames bodies is a contradiction that will fail its own mission. How does the program build genuinely weight-inclusive practice — movement for the joy and capacity of THIS body, not as punishment for its size or a project to shrink it — and win back the millions sport humiliated?

The evidence is messier than either camp admits: fitness and movement carry real health benefits somewhat independent of weight, AND weight-focused messaging often backfires and harms ⚠️ [VITALITY seam, graded honestly]. The program has to hold both without preaching either diet culture or its denial. What's the honest, non-shaming ruling — movement and capacity as the metric, never the number on the scale — and how does the AI coach (SP42) refuse to become a body-surveillance tool?

Aesthetic and weight-class sports — gymnastics, figure skating, wrestling, boxing, dance-as-mastery (SP3) — carry the sharpest body-image and disordered-eating risk in all of sport ⚠️ (SP85 seam). These are also real practices with real mastery that people love. How does the program keep the practice while defusing the body harm structurally — coaching rulings, no weigh-in culture for youth, safeguarding around the mirror?

"The kid picked last" is a design failure, not a fact of nature — the captains'-pick, the cut at nine (SP15), the humiliation ritual baked into how we've always done it. A connection-first program (SP1) can simply refuse it. What are the concrete anti-humiliation design rules — no public cuts for kids, everybody-plays defaults (SP27's no-one-finishes-last), the Mysore room where you only measure against yourself (SP60) — and is "nobody gets picked last, ever" a charter-level promise?

You said every culture has a martial art (SP64), and martial arts already solved visible progression with the belt (SP8) — but their deepest gift may be the pedagogy itself: the dojo's blend of discipline, respect, graded challenge, controlled contact, and the older student teaching the younger (SP16). Is the martial-arts studio the most complete existing model of "practice culture made civic" — and what does the city learn by studying HOW the good dojos teach, not just that they exist?

Martial arts hold a real tension the program must face: controlled violence as a path to non-violence, self-defense as genuine safety (especially for women, kids, the vulnerable ⚠️), and the shadow of dojos that build ego and aggression instead of humility (SP38's "character is conditional"). How does the program tell the forming dojo from the deforming one — and is trained physical confidence a civic good the city should make accessible to everyone who feels unsafe?

The martial-arts world is also full of belt-mill commercialization, fake lineages, and pay-to-progress ⚠️ (SP8's grading poison, SP12's pay-to-play). Meanwhile the authentic lineages are exactly the protocol-and-respect traditions SP66 says not to flatten. How does the program support real martial-arts practice — honoring lineage, resisting the belt-mill — without the city presuming to certify arts it doesn't own?

Drowning is preventable and its risk skews hard by income, newcomer status, and race ⚠️ (SP11) — while swim-lesson waitlists run long and lifeguards are in shortage (SP41). Water competence isn't a sport, it's survival: the ability to not drown is closer to literacy than to athletics. Should "every Torontonian can swim" be a flat civic-right target the way "every kid can read" is — and what does universal water competence cost and take?

A city of lakefront, rivers, ravine creeks, islands, and a harbour with a live swimmability question ⚠️ (SP71) is a city whose relationship to water is broken — we live on a Great Lake and fence ourselves off from it. Earth-as-gym (SP71) means open water as a birthright. How do we reopen the city to its own water — safe open-water swim access, the harbour clean enough (REGENERATION seam), the beaches as practice grounds — and is "swim in your own lake" a civic goal?

Newcomer adults who never learned to swim carry both real danger and real shame around water ⚠️ [NEWCOMERS seam] — and dignity, not embarrassment, is the only way in. Adult learn-to-swim (SP28) is where the program meets the most vulnerable, sometimes with faith-based modesty needs (SP127 seam) around pool access. How does the program build dignified adult and newcomer water competence — women-only hours, patient beginner culture, no shame for starting at 40 — as a first-order safety mission?

Cycling lives on a seam SPORT shares with mobility: it's transport, sport, and practice at once, and the same bike lane serves the commuter, the kid, and the racer [MCI mobility seam]. The infrastructure fight (SP21) is a sport fight and a climate fight (SP121) and an access fight all at once. How does SPORT show up in the streets-and-bikes question — is "every kid can ride, and the city is safe to ride" the water-competence (SP106) of land, and where does SPORT push versus defer to the mobility program?

Climbing gyms became the third-place community centre for a generation that won't attend rec centres (SP22), and climbing, skateboarding, sport climbing and BMX are now Olympic ⚠️ — youth-owned, self-organizing, self-coaching cultures the institutions didn't build and don't control. What does the public option learn from these self-made scenes (SP22) — and how does it support them (more walls, more parks, more free hours) WITHOUT institutionalizing away the youth-ownership that made them work?

Skateparks and parkour spots are where sport is most self-taught, most intergenerational in skill-transfer (the older kid teaching the younger, SP16), and most criminalized — kids chased off ledges, "no skateboarding" signs, the permission gray zone (SP21) ⚠️. These are the purest Mysore rooms (SP5) the city already has and mostly fights. How does the program flip the city's stance from policing youth movement to building for it — and are DIY skate/parkour scenes a model of practice culture the institutions should copy, not tame?

The best youth sports are often the ones adults didn't organize — pick-up basketball, street scenes, the self-run cypher and session. Adult "helping" can kill exactly what made them work (the parkrun-funding warning, SP27). Where's the line between supporting youth-owned sport and colonizing it — how does the program add walls, lights, and hours (SP19) while keeping its hands off the culture, and what's the humility rule for when to just leave it alone?

Refs are quitting faster than they can be replaced because sideline abuse curdled the culture (SP40) — but reframe it: officiating is itself a practice, a mastery, a discipline of judgment under pressure that develops a person as much as playing does. What if the program treated the official as a practitioner on the same development ladder as the athlete (SP16's chains) — every teen a trained official of something — and made refereeing a celebrated civic skill instead of a thankless one?

The sideline-parent problem (SP40) is a spectator-culture problem, and spectator culture is designed, not fated — the quiet-sideline movements, the parent code, silent-support weekends already exist somewhere ⚠️. Fandom is in your trio (SP77), and the abusive sideline is fandom's shadow. Is teaching the city HOW to watch — how to be a good fan, a good sports parent, a good spectator — an actual program deliverable, and what does it look like from the youngest league up?

Sport is the greatest story-engine a city has — the local hero (SP30), the underdog, the comeback, the neighbourhood myth (SP32) — and right now those stories are told by media owned by the same concentrated hands as the teams (SP74) or not told at all. Who tells the city's grassroots sport stories — the masters swimmer, the girls' team that stayed together, the newcomer who learned to skate at 40 (SP108)? Is a public, un-extractive sport-storytelling commons part of making practice sexy (SP29) — and how does the city own its own myths?

Media shapes who plays: what gets broadcast, covered, and celebrated decides which sports and which bodies kids see as possible — women's sport chronically under-covered ⚠️, para sport nearly invisible ⚠️ (SP52), the diaspora's sports (SP13) absent from the sports page. Representation is a pipeline input (SP79), not a nicety. How does the program push visibility for the under-shown — and is "you can't be what you can't see" a design principle for the city's sport media commons?

"Life is 99% practice" is a claim the science of skill acquisition has actually studied — deliberate practice, motor learning, the constraints-led and games-based approaches, the honest and contested state of the "10,000 hours" story ⚠️. If practice is the whole program, the program should know how practice actually works. What does the real skill-acquisition literature (promising, mixed, oversold in places ⚠️) change about how every coach in the city teaches — and does the program publish an honest "how humans actually learn a physical skill" for its whole workforce (SP41)?

The transfer question is the deepest one under your whole thesis (SP55): does mastering body and breath actually build the skills and resilience that carry into mind, spirit, work, and life — or does that beautiful claim mostly fail to transfer the way most far-transfer claims do ⚠️ (the same skepticism SP67 aimed at strategy games)? The program's honesty depends on facing this squarely. What evidence would make the transfer thesis real rather than inspirational — and are you willing to design as if it's true while the factory tests whether it is?

The AI coach (SP42) reshapes the coaching LABOR economy, not just the athlete's experience: if video form-analysis, programming, and feedback go free and automated, what happens to the paid personal trainer, the private-academy coach, the technique specialist whose living depends on scarcity (SP41)? Partners-never-adversaries with a workforce AI is about to disrupt. What's the honest role-transformation deal for coaching labor — AI takes the analysis, the human keeps the love, accountability, and long relationship (SP39) — and who pays the human when the analysis no longer commands a fee?

If elite coaching knowledge becomes free and abundant (SP42), the scarce, valuable, un-automatable thing is the human coach who KNOWS a kid — her body, her history, her fears, her home (the Mysore teacher, SP5). That relationship doesn't scale and shouldn't be automated. How does the program pay for and protect relational coaching at scale — a real living for tens of thousands of neighbourhood coaches whose value is exactly the part AI can't do — and is that the actual jobs program hiding inside SPORT?

Earth-as-gym (SP71) assumes an earth you can safely train on — and the climate is changing what "outdoors" means: worse heat waves, smoke days from distant fires ⚠️, shorter reliable winters (SP20's friluftsliv needs snow), extreme-weather cancellations. The outdoor future is less stable, not more. How does the program design outdoor sport for a destabilizing climate — heat protocols, smoke-day plans, and the honest question of whether the winter-mastery city (SP20) is training for winters that won't reliably come?

Heat is already a safety-and-equity issue: youth practices in dangerous temperatures, no acclimatization protocols, and the poorest neighbourhoods hottest and least shaded ⚠️ [REGENERATION + equity seams]. Sport medicine (SP90) meets climate here. What are the program's heat-safety floors for youth and outdoor practice — and does the tree-canopy-and-shade fight (who gets cool places to play) become a SPORT fight, not just a climate one?

Sport is also a climate ACTOR, not just a victim: the carbon of travel-team culture flying kids across the continent (SP12), mega-event footprints (SP33), the emissions of the facilities themselves ⚠️. A movement built on union-with-nature (SP73) can't quietly wreck the nature. How does the program make its own footprint honest — local-first competition over fly-everywhere travel ball, the 158-Neighbourhood Games (SP32) as the low-carbon answer to the jet-set circuit — and is "practice where you live" a climate virtue too?

Legal sports betting now saturates the broadcast (SP46), the odds are read into the play-by-play, and the same ecosystem addicts the fans it depends on ⚠️ — the addiction seam inverted, and it lands hardest on young men and problem gamblers ⚠️ [VITALITY seam]. Fandom is in your trio (SP77); this is fandom's newest and fastest-growing poison. What is the program's hard firewall — does grassroots and youth sport take zero gambling money, ever, and does the city's own sport media commons (SP115) refuse the odds entirely?

The harm is designed: gamified betting apps, in-play micro-bets, and the same variable-reward machinery that poisons gaming progression (SP8's "which practices should NEVER be gamified") ⚠️. Kids now grow up seeing betting AS part of watching sport. How does the program inoculate young fans — gambling-harm literacy the way we teach any other addiction risk [EDU seam] — and does watching-that-feeds-playing (SP77) become the deliberate counter to watching-that-feeds-betting?

Gambling money is now structurally braided into pro sport's revenue (SP47), so partners-never-adversaries with the pro clubs runs straight into an addiction industry funding the teams. That's a real conflict the program can't wish away. What's the honest ask to the pro ecosystem here — and is refusing gambling sponsorship a line the grassroots commons (SP49) can hold precisely because it's built on different money?

Faith and sport are ancient partners — the fast that includes training, the sabbath as forced recovery (SP63), the Sikh gatka and wrestling akhara, the church-basement badminton (SP13), modesty needs that shape pool and gym access (SP108) ⚠️. Congregations are partners-never- adversaries (the CONNECTION faith-respect pattern) and hold halls, gyms, and belonging the program needs (SP19). How does SPORT partner with the city's faith communities on physical practice — honoring belief, never watering it down, never syncretism-by-design — and is the faith hall one of the biggest dormant practice commons in the city?

University and college sport is a whole tier the bank has barely touched: U SPORTS and OUA programs ⚠️, varsity facilities that sit underused by the surrounding city, the campus as either a talent-factory silo or a public commons. These are massive public-adjacent sport assets (SP11's unlock-what-exists). How does the program treat campus sport — open the varsity pool and track to the neighbourhood, weave college athletes into the coaching chains (SP16), and refuse the US-style scholarship machine that buys performance with young lives (SP26)?

Sport diplomacy is real soft power — the city that hosts a thousand small world championships (SP33) becomes a global practice crossroads, and Toronto's diaspora makes it the natural neutral ground for the world's sports [NEWCOMERS seam, host-never-import]. This is the peaceful, connection-first answer to the mega-event trap. What's the sport-diplomacy strategy — the city as the place the world trains and meets BECAUSE everyone lives here (SP79) — and how does it stay a people's-exchange rather than a nation-branding stunt?

Sport crosses the deepest human lines — the mixed team in a divided neighbourhood, the local peace table (CONNECTION seam) with a ball in it, the practice that unites people politics divides (Yoga = Union, SP54). It can also inflame tribalism (SP77's poison), especially where diaspora communities carry live home-country conflicts (the host-never-import safety constraint). How does the program use sport to unite across difference without becoming a proxy battlefield — and who convenes the mixed practice when the wider conflict is radioactive?

**The base-rate defeat.** Most mass-participation interventions fail to move population activity (SP50), and if, after real investment, Toronto's honest capability census (SP10) — can-you-swim, can-you-ride, can-you-run, minutes-of-practice — shows no movement in the actual population, the program failed at its core promise. What population-level result, measured over what horizon, would you accept as proof the "mastery for everyone" mandate didn't work — and would you shut it down?

**The transfer thesis collapses.** Your deepest claim (SP55, SP118) is that mastering body and breath builds mind and spirit. If the evidence architecture the factory builds shows physical practice does NOT transfer to executive function, emotion regulation, or meaning any better than a coin flip ⚠️, then the philosophical spine cracks. Would you accept that falsification — and does the program survive on movement's direct benefits alone even if the transfer story dies?

**It became an exclusion engine.** If the program, built to win back the picked-last kid (SP99, SP102) and serve those sport wounded (SP51), instead concentrates on the already-fit and already-included — if the gifted pipelines (SP15) quietly recreate the gatekeeping they were meant to end, and the gap between the sporty and the sedentary WIDENS — it became the opposite of its mission. What equity metric, measured how, would prove the program is helping the wrong people, and what stops that before it happens?

**The commons got captured or corrupted.** If the 158-Neighbourhood Games (SP32) turns corporate, the free access hours get monetized (SP49), gambling or junk money (SP124, SP46) buys back in through a side door, or the whole thing becomes a data-surveillance apparatus over people's bodies (SP43, SP100) — the program was captured by exactly what it refused. What are the tripwires that would tell you capture is happening, and who has the authority to pull the plug?

**Personal limits became a harm.** Your "push past your limits" seed (SP59) held against the shadow: if the program's edge-culture produces measurably more RED-S, overtraining, disordered eating, safeguarding failures, or burned-out kids (SP36, SP62, SP85) than the passive city it replaced, then "find your limits" became a machine for hurting people who'd pay anything (SP36). What safety-outcome threshold would prove the edge-pedagogy is doing net harm — and is "personal limits only" strong enough to hold when a kid's own ambition is the thing endangering her?

Where is the Toronto-Waterloo tech ecosystem ACTUALLY at — the honest, measured baseline, not the imagined one: total VC deployed vs the Bay Area and other hubs, the documented anchor- company and scale-up gap (the "we found companies but sell them before they anchor" pattern), net talent retention vs the brain drain south, patents and research output, and the specific places the "undercoordinated and underfunded" diagnosis is TRUE versus where it's a comforting story? Meet the ecosystem where it IS before designing where it could go. *(Where-is-the-ecosystem-ACTUALLY-at; "better than Silicon Valley" as evidence, not assumption.)*

What does the evidence say actually causes the coordination and funding gap — is it capital, or is it fragmentation, a thin domestic customer base, risk-averse procurement, a policy environment, or a culture that sells early? Because the fix for "undercoordinated" (convene, network, commons) is completely different from the fix for "underfunded" (capital), and the fix for "we sell before we scale" is different again — which diagnosis is right, and what does the program build against it?

How do we actually MOBILIZE the ecosystem to build public infrastructure — Civic Tech TO, the incubators, the university labs, the tech-literate youth, the hobbyists — when the thing being built is a public good that doesn't make anyone rich? What does the evidence show about what moves world-class builders onto non-extractive work (mission, status, portfolio, a real user base at city scale, paid fellowships, open-source reputation) versus what civic-tech volunteerism has repeatedly failed to sustain? *(The core "how could we tap them" question, answered with the failure modes attached.)*

How do we make BUILDING public digital infrastructure high-status and aspirational — "sexy" — so that the most talented engineers, designers, and researchers in the corridor compete to contribute to the commons the way they compete for FAANG offers, and so a line on TorontoOS is worth more to a career than a line at a surveillance-ad company? What actually shifts the status game of a tech scene? *(Making the virtue aspirational; the operator's standing "make it sexy" frame applied to civic building.)*

Where is Civic Tech TO and the civic-tech movement ACTUALLY at — measured, not romanticized: what has the community actually shipped and sustained, what died (because most civic apps die), what is its real capacity and burn-out rate, and what is the honest lesson from a decade of civic tech worldwide about why volunteer-built public tools so rarely reach scale or last? What would it take for this to be the exception? *(Civic-tech failure modes as a first-class question.)*

How do we treat the existing tech workforce, the universities, AND the incumbent vendors as partners-never-adversaries in the build — since the corridor's talent is currently employed by the very extractive companies the platform means to displace, and since City IT and existing suppliers will feel threatened by "build from scratch and absorb"? What is the design where their expertise is drawn IN rather than fought, and where the transition dignifies rather than discards them? *(Partners- never-adversaries; tees up T-S3 and T-S6.)*

What is the shared SPINE common to all three faces — the City's operations platform, the politicians↔citizens engagement platform, and the citizens↔citizens platform — and to the CityOS→ProvinceOS→CountryOS→DisasterOS→NeighborhoodOS scaling the operator names? If trust and identity are the common need he flags, what else is genuinely shared (data commons, deliberation, payments/value, notification, consent, discovery) versus what must stay face-specific, so we build one spine and three surfaces rather than three tangled apps? *(The architecture question, from his own framing.)*

How is the TRUST AND IDENTITY layer designed so it is the answer to Sidewalk Toronto rather than a repeat of it — a citizen-owned, sovereign, privacy-preserving identity the person controls, not a platform-owned profile that becomes the surveillance key to everything? What is the honest FOR/AGAINST across the real options (self-sovereign identity / verifiable credentials, a public federated identity, a boring government-issued digital ID), which one actually protects the citizen, and where has each been abused (Aadhaar's exclusion harms, national-ID mission creep)? *(Sidewalk anchor + DPI failure modes + web3-realism converge on the single most load-bearing design choice.)*

How do we build sovereignty-by-architecture so the person owns their data structurally, not by policy promise — since Quayside collapsed exactly because "we'll govern the data responsibly" was never enough: what is the design (personal data stores / data pods, edge/local-first computing, end-to-end encryption, data minimization, the citizen holding the keys) where the platform CANNOT extract or surveil even if a future operator, vendor, or government wanted to? Is that achievable, or is it aspiration dressed as architecture? *(Sovereignty is the product; structural not promissory.)*

What is the honest answer on QUANTUM SECURITY — the operator names it, so: where is post-quantum cryptography ACTUALLY at (the standards that now exist, the real migration timeline), what in a city platform genuinely needs it (long-lived identity, health, sealed ballots — the "harvest-now-decrypt-later" risk) versus where it's a buzzword, and how do we design for crypto-agility so the platform can rotate its cryptography without a rebuild? *(Quantum security as engineering reality, not a buzzword; evidence honesty.)*

How does the DATA COMMONS actually work as a governed public good — who decides what becomes commons vs stays private, how is consent granular and revocable, how does the commons create public value (research, planning, the sovereign-fund thesis from VITALITY) WITHOUT becoming the honeypot that Sidewalk's critics feared? What is the legal container (public data trust, civic data cooperative), and where has a genuine data commons been governed well or badly? *(Data commons as governed institution, not a database.)*

How is the platform ACCESSIBLE and inclusive by law and by design from day one — AODA/WCAG compliance, plain language, every major Toronto language, the digitally-excluded (elders, low-income, disabled, newcomers, the un-connected) reached through human and offline channels — since a "civic platform for all" that only the connected can use is a new inequity, and DPI's worst harm everywhere has been excluding the people who needed it most? *(AODA/accessibility as constraint; DPI exclusion as the failure to design against.)*

What is the actual SYSTEMS MAP — measured, not guessed: what does the City of Toronto (and the GTA municipalities) ACTUALLY run today (311, permits/building, property tax, transit, the ERP/finance backbone, HR, GIS, open-data portal, the myriad department systems), which are aging or locked-in, which contracts and renewal dates constrain the timeline, and which vendors hold the keys? You cannot decide replace-vs-integrate without the real inventory. *(Where-is-Toronto-ACTUALLY- at, applied to the tech estate.)*

What is the honest replace / integrate / leave-alone decision RULE — since "build from scratch and absorb ALL" is how government IT megaprojects fail (the graveyard of billion-dollar rewrites): what is the test that says integrate with a system that works (via open APIs / a strangler-fig pattern) rather than rebuild it, replace only what is genuinely extractive or broken, and never touch what is fine? What does the evidence from failed and successful public-sector modernizations say the rule should be? *(Evidence honesty: government-IT failure as the thing to design against.)*

How do we absorb WITHOUT lock-in — since the whole point is anti-vendor-lock-in, how does the platform itself avoid becoming the new monopoly, the new thing no future city can leave? What is the open-standards, open-data-format, forkable-and-exportable design that guarantees a citizen, a department, or another city can walk away with their data and their workflows intact? *(Anti-lock-in applied reflexively to our own build.)*

How does the MIGRATION happen fast-but-safe without breaking services people depend on — since 311, benefits, permits, and payments cannot go down for a rewrite: what is the sequencing (parallel-run, incremental cutover, real fallbacks) that moves fast where it's safe and slow where lives and livelihoods are on the line, and where is the honest line between "move fast" and "recklessly rip out infrastructure"? *(Fast-but-safe transitions; the operator's standing rule applied to critical systems.)*

What does the City IT organization and the public-sector technologist BECOME in this transition — do the people currently maintaining legacy systems become the stewards, architects, and product owners of the new commons, or do they become the resistance because the project treats them as obstacles? How is their role transformed as an invitation, and how do we work WITH their unions through it? *(Role transformation + partners-never-adversaries; the internal workforce the build depends on.)*

How do we run "build from scratch and absorb" without repeating Sidewalk's central mistake — a private-led megaproject that promised the city everything and controlled the terms? What is the governance where the build is public-led, publicly owned, incrementally proven, and reversible at every stage, so the city is never again in a position where a single builder holds the leverage? *(Sidewalk anchor applied to the delivery model itself, not just the data.)*

What does "1–3M conversations between the mayor and all the citizens" actually MEAN mechanically — since one human cannot have three million conversations, the honest design is the question: opinion-clustering and consensus-surfacing at scale (the Polis / vTaiwan model the existing pilot already implements) that finds where the city actually agrees, feeding a much smaller number of real human deliberations, with the mayor genuinely IN the loop — not a chatbot wearing the mayor's face. Where exactly does the human stay central, and where does AI only assist? *(Builds on the DELIB pilot; AI-as-facilitator-never-replacement made concrete.)*

How do the 10,000 purok-level conversations ROLL UP without the human texture being crushed into a number — what is the design where a block's real deliberation is aggregated up to the ward, the city, the GTA, and (per the CountryOS scaling) beyond, in a way that preserves dissent, minority positions, and the "why," rather than flattening everything into a majority bar chart? How does roll-up inform without laundering local voice into false consensus? *(Deliberation-at-scale with fidelity; the roll-up is where scale usually kills nuance.)*

Where is the line the AI facilitator must NEVER cross — since the operator's hard constraint is "without losing the human touch": AI may cluster, translate, summarize, surface, and schedule; AI may NOT decide, vote, manufacture consensus, or be presented as a participant with a stake. How do we encode that line so no future operator can quietly move it, and how is every AI-summarized or AI-modeled output LABELED as such so citizens always know what a human said versus what a model inferred? *(The DELIB validity rule: simulated is always labeled; only real deliberation confers mandate.)*

How do we prevent deliberation-at-scale from being CAPTURED, astroturfed, brigaded, or Sybil-attacked — since any system that "rolls up" to influence power becomes a target: what is the design (the sovereign identity layer from T-S2, sortition/random-sample panels, rate-limiting, bot detection) that keeps the loudest, the best-funded, and the fake from dominating, and keeps the quiet majority and the marginalized genuinely heard? *(Elections-integrity-adjacent; the failure mode that discredits every civic platform if unsolved.)*

How does mass deliberation actually change a DECISION — the honesty question civic tech usually ducks: what is the binding relationship between what the 10,000 puroks deliberate and what the City actually does, given that council, the City Manager, provincial law, and budgets hold real authority? Is this consultation theatre with better graphics, or does it have teeth (participatory budgeting with real dollars, citizen assemblies with a mandate, published must-respond obligations)? Where has digital democracy genuinely shifted power, and where was it a pressure valve? *(Digital-democracy evidence + failure modes; jurisdiction honesty on where authority actually sits.)*

How does the platform reach the people who will NEVER be on an app — since a deliberation system that hears only the connected produces a confidently-wrong "will of the city": what are the offline, in-person, translated, doorstep, and community-broker channels (the purok facilitators themselves as humans) that bring the disconnected in, so the roll-up represents the whole city, not its online sliver? *(Connection as the underlying answer; the human facilitator is the feature, not a cost to automate away.)*

What does it mean for TorontoOS to be the delivery layer for EVERY program — VITALITY, NEWCOMERS, EDU, deliberation, the puroks, the research library — rather than each building its own silo? What is the shared services model (identity, notifications, consent, payments, deliberation, data commons) every program plugs into, so a Torontonian has ONE trusted front door to all of it, and what is the honest risk of that single front door becoming a single point of control or failure? *(The delivery-layer thesis + its concentration risk.)*

What ARE the right role-appropriate dashboards — genuinely different views for the City Manager (whole-of-city operations), the Mayor (political and public accountability), a Department Head (their unit's KPIs and bottlenecks), the Public (radical transparency, plain-language), and the Unions (workforce conditions, safety, staffing) — built on the same underlying truth so no one gets a private, flattering version? What is the design where everyone sees the SAME reality, sliced for their role? *(The operator's dashboard question, made concrete and honest.)*

How do we make the city's operations RADICALLY transparent to the public — real KPIs, real spending, real service levels, real wait times, updated live — as the anti-Sidewalk move (the public can see everything the platform does), while protecting the legitimately private (personal data, security-sensitive operations, HR)? Where is the honest line between transparency-as-accountability and transparency-as-exposure, and who draws it? *(Transparency as the trust-building product; privacy/security as the constraint.)*

How do we stop the dashboards from being GAMED or turned into a surveillance-management weapon — since the moment a KPI has power, it gets juked (Goodhart), and since "everything each department is doing" can become a tool to surveil and speed-up the workforce the unions represent? How do we make sport and movement a LIFELONG habit rather than something that ends at graduation — since the drop-off in physical activity after school is one of the most predictable and damaging health patterns there is? How do we 100x clubs and community sport the operator asks for — what is the actual math and design of going from scarce, gated, expensive facilities to abundant, cheap, everywhere ones (school gyms open evenings and weekends, park programming, pick-up culture, low-cost community clubs), and where do the real bottlenecks sit (facilities, cost, coaching, permits, insurance, time)? What is the fastest path to abundance? *(Practice over theory: real clubs people actually join this month.)*

How do we make DISCIPLINE and self-mastery aspirational — "sexy" — so that showing up, progressing, and mastering a hard thing is high-status and celebrated across a whole culture, not a grind people dread or a flex only the privileged can afford? What does the evidence on habit formation, mastery motivation, and intrinsic vs extrinsic reward say actually builds a lifelong practice, and what does the program design so the win is the doing, not the medal? *(Making virtue aspirational; composes with the EDU "self-discipline sexy" frame.)*

How do we design HEALTHY competition and visible PROGRESSION — leagues, ladders, belts, levels, the "Game of Life" progression the movement uses elsewhere — so competition motivates and connects rather than excludes and shames, and so progress is legible and rewarding at every level from beginner to master? Where does competition help (motivation, community, mastery) and where does it harm (dropout of the less-gifted, injury, obsession), and what is the design that captures the first without the second?

How do we reach the people sport currently EXCLUDES — women and girls in the activities where they drop out, disabled people, larger-bodied people, older adults, low-income families priced out, and the un-athletic who were shamed out young — so "lifelong sport for all" is real rather than a program for the already-fit? What does the evidence say brings the excluded IN, and where is Toronto ACTUALLY failing them now? *(Equity and dignity: sport for every body.)*

How do we build self-mastery beyond sport — breath, cold, strength, skill, focus, the disciplines of the body and attention the "biohacking" culture the operator gestures at explores — in an evidence-honest way that separates what's genuinely supported from what's hype and hazard, and that democratizes the practices rather than leaving them a status game for the wealthy? Where is the line between empowering self-mastery and selling unproven self-optimization? *(Frontier-but-honest; composes with V-S7.)*

What is the honest FOR/AGAINST on being a bleeding-edge health city — FOR: earlier access to genuine breakthroughs, a research and innovation magnet, hope for the currently-untreatable, and the leadership the operator envisions. AGAINST: unproven interventions on real bodies, the DIY- biohacking harm frontier, snake-oil dressed as innovation, and the equity risk that the frontier serves the rich and the desperate first? What is the frame that lets Toronto move fast on the edge while the protection is structural, not aspirational?

How do we run frontier health under a two-key ethics gate the movement cannot waive — since "protecting people" is only real if there's a mechanism no enthusiasm can override: what is the ethics, consent, and safety architecture (independent review, informed and revocable consent, no vulnerable-population testing without the highest safeguards, honest adverse-event reporting) that gates anything experimental touching a real person? *(Two-key ethics gate, non-waivable.)*

How do we protect people from the FRONTIER'S dark side while embracing its light — the unregulated longevity clinics, the direct-to-consumer tests of dubious value, the supplement and peptide grey market, the "wellness" grift that preys on fear and hope? What does honest consumer protection and evidence-literacy look like in a city that also wants to lead on genuine innovation, and how does it avoid becoming either a rubber stamp or a wall? *(Corporate-gates and testing-honesty compose here.)*

How do we build the evidence-honesty muscle at population scale — since the whole frontier question turns on a city that can tell a real breakthrough from a hyped one: what does it take to make the public (and the program itself) genuinely literate in evidence grades, trial quality, and the difference between "promising" and "proven," so people can navigate the frontier without being either credulous or paralyzed? *(Practice over theory; making evidence-literacy a civic skill.)*

Where are the corporate gates ACTUALLY located, argued from published evidence at the institutional level — the documented patterns in pharmaceutical pricing and patent strategy, the food industry's role in the ultra-processed-food and chronic-disease burden, the consolidation of primary care and pharmacy, the paywalls on nutrition and health knowledge? How does the program name the SYSTEM-level failures precisely, from the record, without ever authoring an unverified claim or turning the nurses, pharmacists, farmers, and grocers inside those systems into the enemy? *(Pointer-never-author; institutional level only; workforce as partner.)*

How do we break the gates by BUILDING alternatives rather than only attacking incumbents — community-owned food production and distribution, generic and compounded medicine access, open health knowledge, cooperative pharmacies and clinics, public-interest research — so that the gates fall because something better and community-owned outcompetes them? What is the build-not-just-fight design, and where has it worked?

What does FOOD AS MEDICINE mean built as real infrastructure — since the Hippocrates line is quoted everywhere and practiced almost nowhere: produce prescriptions, medically-tailored meals, teaching kitchens, food-is-medicine programs integrated into care, and the evidence for each? Where is the honest line between the genuine evidence (diet's role in chronic disease is among the strongest in medicine) and the overreach (food cannot cure everything, and "let food be thy medicine" has been used to sell dangerous nonsense and to blame the sick)? *(Food-as-medicine with evidence discipline; never medical advice.)*

How do we fix the FOOD ENVIRONMENT that makes the healthy choice the hard choice — since personal nutrition advice is nearly useless against a food system engineered for overconsumption: what is the municipal and community lane on food deserts and swamps, on the affordability and accessibility of real food, on local and community food production, so that the default becomes healthy rather than the exception? Where is Toronto ACTUALLY at on food access by neighbourhood, and who profits from it staying broken? *(Where-is-Toronto-ACTUALLY-at; equity constraint.)*

How do we take the money and the perverse incentives OUT of the system honestly — since much of the corporate gate is an incentive structure that profits from sickness and scarcity: where does the money actually flow in food and medicine and health today, who loses income if the incentives flip toward prevention and access, and how do we design that transition so the honest workers land somewhere better rather than being thrown out with the rent-seekers? *(Take the money out; honest costs; fast-but-safe.)*

How do we do all of this WITH the health and food workforce as partners — the farmers, grocers, pharmacists, dietitians, nurses, and physicians whose livelihoods are inside the system being reformed — so that breaking the corporate gates never means breaking the people, and the reform is something they help lead because it dignifies their work? *(Partners-never-adversaries, the operator's and the movement's standing rule.)*

How do we PREVENT mental illness from developing at population scale — since the operator asks for prevention first, and since the evidence points upstream to connection, security, purpose, early-life conditions, and belonging (the very things this whole program builds)? Where is Toronto ACTUALLY at on mental-health burden by age and population, what are the highest-ROI upstream interventions the evidence supports, and how does the program measure prevention (the hardest thing to prove because success is an absence)? *(Prevention as the first move; dignity throughout.)*

How do we RESOLVE the mental illness people already carry — building access to effective, timely, affordable, culturally-matched, and de-stigmatized care, since the operator asks for both prevention AND resolution? Where are the honest gaps (wait times, cost, cultural and language barriers, the crisis-only system that catches people too late), and what is the design that meets people early and holds them with dignity rather than only in emergencies? *(Dignity center: describe the condition, never stigmatize the person.)*

How do we recognize and work with SPIRITUAL health through secular access — since the operator asks for it directly and the evidence on meaning, ritual, contemplative practice, and belonging for wellbeing is real, but the movement is never doctrinal: what does it look like to honour the wisdom lineages (contemplative, meditative, ceremonial) and the human need for meaning and transcendence, offered as secular-accessible practice available to all, with Indigenous spiritual practice represented only through published Indigenous voices on their own protocol, never appropriated? *(Spiritual health via secular access; Indigenous content protocol-flagged.)*

What does the EVIDENCE actually show on psychedelic-assisted and other emerging therapies — argued honestly, separating the genuine clinical-trial signal (the published research on psilocybin, MDMA, ketamine, and others for specific conditions) from the hype, the harms, and the populations for whom these carry serious risk? What is the honest state of the science, and what does the program refuse to overstate? *(Drugs-as-medicine = trial evidence, honestly graded; never medical advice.)*

How do we engage "recognize illegal drugs as medicine" within REGULATORY and JURISDICTIONAL reality — since drug scheduling is FEDERAL, not municipal: what are the actual legal pathways that exist (Health Canada's Special Access Program, Section 56 exemptions, clinical trials, the documented history of Toronto's and Canada's own policy decisions), how does a city work within them and advocate to change them through legitimate channels, and how does the program discuss all of this with zero advocacy of illegal activity? *(Regulatory + jurisdiction honesty; zero illegal-activity advocacy.)*

How do we hold the HARM-REDUCTION evidence with dignity and honesty — since addiction is a health condition, not a moral failing, and since the harm-reduction literature (supervised consumption, naloxone, safer supply where evidence exists, treatment-on-demand) is contested in public debate but has a real evidence base? What does the evidence actually show, argued straight, and how does the program center the dignity and lives of people who use drugs while being honest about what's proven, what's debated, and what remains a federal and provincial jurisdiction? *(Dignity for people who use drugs; evidence honesty; FOR/AGAINST where the evidence is genuinely contested.)*

How do we run anything psychedelic-adjacent or touching people in crisis under a two-key ethics gate the movement cannot waive — since these are the highest-risk interventions touching the most vulnerable people: what is the consent, screening, safety, and independent-review architecture that gates any program in this stream, exactly as the vulnerable-population gates protect minors and frail elders elsewhere in the series? *(Two-key ethics gate, non-waivable; vulnerable-population safeguarding.)*

Who GOVERNS the vitality commons — since the sovereign-wealth-fund, the centralized data, the collective-profit thesis, and the local-ownership design all concentrate real power and money: what is the governance structure that keeps the commons genuinely community-controlled (accountable, transparent, democratically governed, capture-resistant against private buyout, insurer access, state overreach, and its own future leaders), and where has anything at this scale been governed well or badly? *(The central power question, held honestly.)*

How do we hold the HONEST costs and the honest ledger — since a city cannot test everyone in every way, prescribe nature and connection at scale, break the corporate gates, and lead the frontier all at once without hard tradeoffs: what does this actually cost, what does it save (and how sure are we, given the screening-harms and community-care-savings debates the series has already stress- tested), and what does the program refuse to promise it can afford? *(Take-the-money-out and honest-costs discipline; no invented savings.)*

How does the program engage the hardest public DEBATES without ducking them — the honest FOR/AGAINST on comprehensive testing, on data centralization, on harm reduction, on medical tourism, on frontier medicine — in language that survives a hostile fact-checker AND leaves every reader (including the sick, the addicted, the frail, and the poor) feeling described with dignity, locating failures in system design rather than in the character of the people the system failed?

What are the genuine high-ROI vitality wins — measured, not assumed — where a dollar spent on connection, prevention, movement, nature, or early access returns multiples in avoided illness, avoided hospitalization, and years of good life? What does the program MEASURE as success, and what does it refuse to target directly so the metric doesn't corrupt the mission (Goodhart), given how easily "healthiest and happiest" numbers can be gamed?

How do we run the whole thing as PRACTICE, not theory — since "life is 99% practice" — so the program is measured by Torontonians who ACTUALLY danced this week, ACTUALLY got outside, ACTUALLY made a friend, ACTUALLY moved their body, ACTUALLY reached care early — real events in real weeks, not frameworks and pledges? What is the practice-culture design that keeps this program from becoming another well-worded wellness report? *(Practice over theory.)*

How do we guarantee the program is done BY the people, not TO them — guarding against the trap where a well-meaning designer builds a vitality program for a community without that community holding the pen, the data, the fund, and the payroll — especially for the neighbourhoods, the racialized, the disabled, the poor, and the Indigenous communities the health system has historically harmed and who have the most reason to distrust it? What is the "nothing about us without us" governance, applied to health? *(Dignity, trust, and community control as the design foundation.)*

How does the movement itself stay HEALTHY — since a program preaching vitality, connection, and sustainable practice will fail its own thesis if it burns out its people, and since the health workforce and organizers it depends on are already exhausted? What does it look like to build a vitality movement that practices what it prescribes on its own members first?
